title: The ladder strategy: buying bonds of different terms
subtitle: Bond laddering strategy
openingQuestion: Instead of putting all 500 million dong into a single 5-year bond, an investor splits it into 5 portions of 100 million each, buying bonds with 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5-year terms. What is this strategy called, and what is its main benefit?
openingOptions: 'Sector diversification' - cutting credit risk across industries
Just buying assorted terms at random, with no strategy name
'Dollar-cost averaging', as with buying stocks each month
The ladder strategy - a portion of capital matures every year
explanation: The ladder strategy means splitting invested capital into several portions and buying bonds with maturities spread evenly over time (for example 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 years). This way, a portion of capital always matures every year, which can be reinvested at the current rate, reducing the risk of reinvesting all the capital at once right when rates happen to be low, while still maintaining steady liquidity.

diagram.label: Split capital into several equal portions
Reinvest that portion at the current rate - risk isn't concentrated at one moment

realWorldExample.company: An individual investor building a ladder with government bonds and term deposits
realWorldExample.description: A common way to apply laddering in Vietnam for a beginner, even without access to many types of bonds, is to combine 1, 2, and 3-year government bonds or certificates of deposit at the same time, instead of putting everything into a single 3-year savings account. When the 1-year portion matures, the investor checks the market rate at that time to decide on reinvesting for a new term (usually the longest term in the ladder to keep the structure intact), instead of having to guess future rates from the very start.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of a bond ladder strategy?
options: Reducing the risk of having to reinvest all your capital at once at an unfavorable rate
No longer needing to track rate movements at all
Guaranteeing a yield that's always higher than the market level
Fully eliminating the issuer's default risk
quiz.explanation: A ladder spreads out maturity dates, so an investor doesn't have to reinvest all their capital at once right when rates happen to be low, while also having a portion of capital mature each year, ready to use if liquidity is needed.

quiz.question: When a bond in the ladder matures, what does an investor usually do to maintain the ladder structure?
options: Withdraw all money out of the bond market and stop running the ladder strategy entirely
Buy a new bond at the longest term, moving the just-matured rung to the back of the line
Leave the money idle in the account, without investing it, and this protection only holds for the specific rungs that have not yet reached maturity
Use all the matured money to buy stocks instead
quiz.explanation: To keep the ladder structure continuous, when the shortest-term bond matures, an investor usually reinvests that money into a new bond at the longest term in the ladder, keeping the portfolio's rungs evenly spread across time.

quiz.question: You have 500 million dong and build a 5-rung ladder. What does the initial structure look like?
options: Split in half: half at a 1-year term and the other half at a 5-year term
The entire 500 million goes into a 5-year bond to earn the highest rate
100 million per rung, with terms of 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 years spread evenly
100 million per rung, but all of them mature in year five
quiz.explanation: The key point is that the maturity dates are spread evenly, not just the money. After year one, the 1-year rung matures and you buy a new 5-year term - from then on, exactly one rung comes due every year, and the structure sustains itself.

quiz.question: How does a ladder differ from concentrating everything into a single 5-year term?
options: A ladder is exempt from tax on coupon interest because the capital is split into several rungs
A ladder always delivers a higher average yield than concentrating into one long term
A ladder entirely eliminates default risk by splitting capital across several issuers
A ladder gives steady liquidity and doesn't bet everything on a single rate level
quiz.explanation: Concentrating everything into one term means your entire capital is locked to the rate level of a single day - the day you bought. A ladder spreads that decision out over several years, so you're never entirely right, but also never entirely wrong.

quiz.question: Rates fall sharply and stay low for several years. How does a ladder perform?
options: It still maintains a higher average yield than the market thanks to the long rungs bought earlier
Every rung in the ladder instantly switches to the new lower rate that same year
The ladder automatically stops and all capital must be withdrawn into cash
The ladder suffers noticeably more than concentrating everything into a short term
quiz.explanation: The long rungs, bought at the old rate, keep paying a high coupon for many years, so the ladder's average yield lags the market on the way down. In exchange, when rates rise, the ladder also climbs more slowly - that's the price of stability.

quiz.question: Does a ladder protect an investor from default risk?
options: Yes, because the capital is split into small pieces, so any one default is insignificant
No - a ladder splits by term, not by bond issuer
Yes, because the short rungs mature before the issuer can run into financial trouble
No, but that's only true for a ladder with fewer than five different terms
quiz.explanation: A ladder addresses interest rate risk and reinvestment risk, not credit risk. If all five rungs are bonds from the same company and that company defaults, you lose all five rungs. To hedge against that, you need to diversify across issuers.

keyTakeaways: A ladder is a strategy of splitting capital into several portions, buying bonds with maturities spread evenly over time instead of concentrating everything into one term
Main benefit: reducing the risk of reinvesting all capital at once at an unfavorable rate, while having steady liquidity every year
When a rung matures, it's usually reinvested at the longest term in the ladder, to keep the structure continuous over time

practicePrompt.question: You're running a ladder strategy with 5 bonds of 1-5 year terms. The 1-year bond has just matured. What should you do to maintain the ladder structure?
options: Use the just-matured money to buy a new bond at the 5-year term (the longest in the ladder), keeping the rungs evenly maintained year after year
Keep that money as cash and don't buy any more bonds, since the ladder has already done its job, a move that would also make sense if the bond market had shown no volatility at all that year
Use the entire amount to buy another 1-year bond identical to the one that just matured, to keep the original allocation unchanged
Move the entire amount into stocks instead, since current bond rates aren't attractive enough to keep running the ladder
practicePrompt.explanation: Reinvesting at the longest term in the ladder keeps the rung structure continuous over time - this is how the strategy is meant to operate.

summary.keyIdea: A ladder is a strategy of splitting capital into several portions, buying bonds with maturities spread evenly over time instead of concentrating everything into one term
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a line to recite rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: Main benefit: reducing the risk of reinvesting all capital at once at an unfavorable rate, while having steady liquidity every year

application.title: Sketch out a ladder
application.message: Suppose you have 100 million dong; try splitting it into 4-5 portions with different maturities (1, 2, 3, 4, 5 years) to picture how a ladder strategy is built.
application.secondary: Just sketching it on paper is enough to understand the logic - no need to actually do it yet.

sections.text: If you have a large amount of money you want to invest in bonds but aren't sure which term to choose, there's a simple strategy that saves you from having to guess the right rate timing: the ladder strategy.

A ladder is a strategy of splitting the total capital into several equal portions, and buying bonds with different maturities, spread evenly over time. For example, with 500 million dong, instead of buying a single 5-year bond, you split it into 5 portions of 100 million each, buying bonds with 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5-year terms. The result is that a portion of capital always matures every year.

sections.label: Why it's called a 'ladder'
sections.text: If you plot the maturity dates on a timeline, you'll see the maturity points lined up in rungs spaced evenly by year - like a ladder, with a new rung maturing every year.
What problem does a ladder solve

items: If you concentrate all your capital into a single term, you have to 'bet' on one single decision at one single moment - if rates happen to be low then, your entire capital gets 'locked' at that low yield for the whole long term
With a ladder, only a small portion of capital matures each year, so if rates are low that year, only that portion is affected, while the rest still enjoys the yield locked in earlier
A ladder also gives you steady liquidity: money matures ready to use every year, so you don't have to sell a bond before maturity (potentially at a loss) if you need cash urgently

left.label: Concentrating into 1 term
left.text: Simple, but higher risk: if it happens to be locked in right when rates are low, all the capital gets stuck at that low yield for the entire long term, with no liquidity in between.

right.label: The ladder strategy
right.text: Spreads risk over several points in time, always has a portion maturing each year to reinvest at the current rate, while maintaining more flexible liquidity.

sections.text: The ladder strategy suits an investor with a relatively large amount of capital who wants safe long-term investing but doesn't want to 'bet' everything on a single term decision. It's also a common strategy for someone approaching retirement, wanting a steady annual stream of maturing money to spend without having to sell assets early.

lines: A ladder is a way of splitting timing risk when investing in bonds, by spreading maturities across several years.
This strategy fits when you have large capital, want safety, and don't want to have to guess the single best moment to invest it all at once.
